summary:
We developed the “Analog Finder”, a tool that finds places on Earth that most closely resemble potential base sites on the Moon and Mars. It compares 101,278 land cells on Earth (about 37 km each) with the “fingerprint” of 14 target sites: nine Artemis candidate regions and Shackleton on the Moon, plus Arcadia Planitia, Deuteronilus Mensae, Jezero and Gale on Mars.

The comparison covers eleven dimensions, including slope, relief, sun elevation, temperature, precipitation, vegetation, air pressure, ground ice, albedo and dust. The data comes mainly from NASA (MODIS, MERRA-2, LOLA, MOLA, PDS). Each cell scores 0 to 100 points per dimension, and a sensitivity analysis checks how stable the ranking is.

The best matches are the Kunlun and Tibesti Mountains for Mars and Ellesmere Island for the Moon. Known analogs such as the Atacama, Haughton Crater and Svalbard rank near the top, which supports the method. The result is an interactive map, and a finer version with 5 km cells is already being developed.
details:
What it does
The Analog Finder answers one question: where on Earth is most like a future base site on the Moon or Mars? We describe 27 target sites with a common “fingerprint”. On Mars these are 14 sites, including the Perseverance, Curiosity and InSight landing sites and the ice-rich base candidates Arcadia Planitia and Deuteronilus Mensae. At the lunar south pole these are 13 sites, including NASA’s Artemis III candidate regions, Shackleton and Cabeus. We then compare every patch of Earth’s land (8.9 million cells of about 5 km, with climate data from 2003–2024) against each fingerprint.

How it works
Each cell is scored on terrain (slope, relief), surface material (albedo, thermal inertia), temperature, dryness, atmosphere, dust and wind, ground ice, vegetation and sunlight. The comparison is designed to be fair across worlds. Quantities measured the same way are compared value against value: terrain is processed with the same code on all three bodies. Values from different instruments are compared by rank. Conditions Earth never reaches, such as a vacuum or 6 hPa air pressure, count as “the closer, the better”. Every value carries a reliability grade that sets its weight. The best matches are checked in three ways: a robustness test under 1,000 random weightings, site profiles with Landsat imagery and 90 m terrain, and a literature check of the newly found sites.

Benefits and impact
Analog sites are where astronauts train, rovers and habitats are tested, and scientists study Mars- and Moon-like processes. Until now, analogs have mostly been chosen by expert judgement. Our tool makes the choice transparent and reproducible. For every match it explains what fits and where the analogy breaks. It also points to promising sites that are not yet established analogs. Without knowing them in advance, it found well-known analogs such as the Qaidam Basin, the Atacama, Salar de Uyuni, Axel Heiberg Island and Haughton Crater, which supports the method.

Results
The best Mars analogs lie on the Tibetan Plateau and in the Qaidam Basin, followed by the Andes and the Sahara. The best analogs for the lunar south pole are the ice-free polar deserts of the Canadian High Arctic and North Greenland.

Tools and data
We used Python (NumPy, pandas, xarray, rasterio, GDAL, scikit-learn) and NASA’s APIs: CMR via earthaccess for the Earth data, and the PDS Registry and PDS Geosciences ODE for the Moon and Mars. The datasets are:

  • Earth: MODIS, MERRA-2, GPM IMERG and NASA GIBS, plus ESA’s Copernicus DEM for terrain.
  • Moon: LRO LOLA and Diviner.
  • Mars: MGS MOLA and TES.

The web app is a single HTML file and runs without a server. We used Anthropic’s Claude (Claude Code) to write and run much of the code under our direction. All results were checked against the data, maps and satellite images.

What makes it creative
Users pick a target on a Mars or Moon map and immediately see a world map of similarity. They can set their own weights, filter by environment type, compare up to three sites side by side and inspect each match in satellite view.

Factors we considered
Fair comparison between instruments on different bodies, data reliability, robustness of the ranking, and stating the limits openly. No place on Earth reproduces low gravity, vacuum or space radiation.
